questions.stem: In a series circuit, the supply voltage is:

options.explanation: The loop divides the supply voltage among everything in it.
That is parallel behaviour; series shares the voltage out.

options.text: multiplied by the number of components
options.explanation: The supply is fixed; the components divide it, not multiply it.
Each component takes its own share of the supply.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps in series across a 12 V battery take:

options.explanation: Only in parallel would each see the full supply voltage.
Identical components split the 12 V supply equally: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 V.
Nothing can give out more voltage than the supply holds.
That would be quartering the supply, not halving it.

questions.stem: Two different resistors sit in series across a supply. The larger resistance takes:

options.text: the smaller share of the voltage
options.explanation: The shares follow the resistances, not the reverse.
Every series component takes some share of the supply.

options.text: the same share as the other resistor
options.explanation: Different resistances break the equal-share case.

options.text: the larger share of the voltage
options.explanation: In series, more resistance claims more of the supply voltage.

questions.stem: In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is:

options.explanation: Each branch connects straight across the supply, so it takes the full voltage.
Halving belongs to two identical series components, not parallel branches.
Parallel branches do not divide the voltage; each gets all of it.
Every branch sees the supply voltage, wherever it sits.

questions.stem: Two lamps are wired in parallel across a 6 V supply. The voltage across each lamp is:

options.explanation: Parallel lamps do not halve the supply.
Both lamps take the full 6 V across them.
The supply cannot deliver more than it holds.
A connected branch always sees the supply voltage.

questions.stem: State how the supply voltage is divided in a series circuit, and what each branch gets in a parallel circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: In series the supply voltage is shared among the components; in parallel every branch receives the full supply voltage.

questions.stem: Two resistors of different size sit in series. Which one takes the larger voltage share?
questions.modelAnswer: The resistor with the larger resistance takes the larger share of the supply voltage.

questions.stem: Explain why two identical lamps in series each take exactly half the battery's voltage.
questions.modelAnswer: Identical lamps have equal resistance, so the shared voltage divides equally between them — each receives half of the supply voltage.

questions.stem: A 9 V battery drives two different resistors in series. The first resistor takes 3.6 V. Find the voltage across the second resistor.
questions.modelAnswer: The shares must sum to the supply: 9 − 3.6 = 5.4 V across the second resistor.

questions.stem: One advantage of connecting lamps in series is:

options.text: each lamp can be switched separately
options.explanation: Separate switching is the parallel advantage; series couples everything to one switch.

options.text: a broken lamp does not affect the others
options.explanation: In series one break stops the whole loop.
A single loop needs less wiring than a branch array.

options.text: each lamp gets the full voltage
options.explanation: Series lamps share the supply voltage between them.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of series lighting is that:

options.text: one failed lamp stops all of them working
options.explanation: The single loop is broken by any failed component.

options.text: the lamps cannot share the voltage
options.explanation: Sharing the voltage is exactly what series lamps do.
Series needs just one switch for everything.

options.text: the current splits unfairly between lamps
options.explanation: Series current never splits at all — it is one loop.

questions.stem: Domestic lighting is wired in parallel mainly because:

options.explanation: Parallel needs more wiring; that is its accepted cost.
Lamps take current whenever they are lit.

options.text: a single switch controls every room
options.explanation: Homes want the opposite: per-room control.

options.text: each light can be controlled and one failure leaves the rest lit
options.explanation: Independent switching plus failure isolation is exactly why homes choose parallel.

questions.stem: If one branch of a parallel circuit breaks:

options.explanation: That is the series failure mode.
Each branch is independent across the supply, so the rest stay lit.
The supply voltage stays at its set value.
The topology of the circuit does not change when a branch fails.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of parallel circuits compared with series is:

options.explanation: Individual control is the parallel advantage.

options.text: more wiring and connections are required
options.explanation: Branching costs extra wires, which makes setup more complicated.
All parallel branches receive the same, full supply voltage.
Parallel branches survive each other's failures.

questions.stem: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a series lighting circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: Advantage: a single switch and fewer wires control the whole loop. Disadvantage: if one lamp fails, every lamp goes out.

questions.stem: Name the circuit type used for domestic lighting and one reason why.
questions.modelAnswer: Parallel — every lamp can be switched on its own, and one failed lamp leaves the rest working.

questions.stem: Explain why a broken lamp in a parallel string does not darken the room's other lamps.
questions.modelAnswer: Each lamp sits on its own branch connected straight across the supply, so the remaining branches still receive the full supply voltage and keep working.

questions.stem: A classroom wants lamps that can each be switched separately and stay lit if one fails. Which arrangement should be chosen, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Wire the lamps in parallel: each branch takes its own switch for individual control, and a failed branch leaves the others working.
